```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)
options(width = 72)
has_fmrihrf <- requireNamespace("fmrihrf", quietly = TRUE)
note <- function(pkg) {
  cat(
    '<p class="chunk-note">The next chunk needs the <code>', pkg,
    "</code> package, which is not installed, so it was not run.</p>",
    sep = ""
  )
}
```

An fMRI array is only as good as what you know about its rows and columns.
Analyses go wrong when that knowledge slips: a matrix masked with one mask is
read with another mask's voxel order, two runs are concatenated and the run
boundary is forgotten when the design is built, or parcel means are saved
without the atlas their columns came from. Nothing in a bare matrix catches
these mistakes.

`fmridataset` keeps that knowledge attached. Its container, the `fmri_frame`,
holds one or more arrays of observations (rows, usually volumes) by features
(columns: voxels, vertices, parcels, or components), together with a table
describing each observation, a *feature space* describing each column, and
stable IDs on both axes. Operations that would break the link between the
numbers and their meaning are refused rather than guessed. If you know
Bioconductor's `SummarizedExperiment`, the idea is the same: assays plus
annotations, with observations as rows.

This vignette covers the everyday operations. The other vignettes go further:

- `vignette("feature-spaces")`: volumes, surfaces, parcels, and latent
  components, and moving data between them.
- `vignette("studies")`: subjects, runs, and other entities, and studies that
  link several frames.
- `vignette("persistence-and-import")`: importing fMRIPrep output, saving
  frames to disk, and what makes two frames the same.

```{r}
library(fmridataset)
```

## From your data to a frame

Most frames start from files. `read_nifti_bold()` opens one NIfTI file per
run, keeps the voxels inside a mask, and records the runs and TR. It reads the
headers and the mask but no BOLD values: those stay on disk until you ask for
them.

```{r nifti, eval = FALSE}
bold <- read_nifti_bold(
  c("sub-01_run-1_bold.nii.gz", "sub-01_run-2_bold.nii.gz"),
  mask = "sub-01_brain_mask.nii.gz",
  TR = 2
)
```

For fMRIPrep output, `read_bids_bold()` finds the runs, masks, and events for
you; `vignette("persistence-and-import")` shows it on a small example tree.
Data already in R work too. `as_fmri_frame()` accepts a time-by-feature
matrix, `neuroim2` `NeuroVec` volumes with a mask, or a latent decomposition.

```{r as-fmri-frame}
set.seed(1)
quick <- as_fmri_frame(
  matrix(rnorm(6 * 4), nrow = 6, ncol = 4),
  TR = 2,
  run_length = c(4, 2),
  censor = 3 # exclude the third volume
)
quick
observations(quick)
```

Each row got an ID derived from its run and position, plus the run, the
position within the run, the TR, and the censoring flag. The printout lists
the frame's assays (the arrays of numbers), the *active* assay that functions
use when you do not name one, and the type of feature space.

## What a frame holds

The constructors above all call `fmri_frame()`, which you can use directly. It
needs at least one assay, an observation table with a unique `.obs_id` per
row, and a feature space. Here the space is a tiny 3 by 3 by 2 volume and the
rows are eight volumes from two runs.

```{r build}
voxels <- volume_space(dim = c(3, 3, 2), template = "toy")
voxels

bold <- matrix(
  round(rnorm(8 * n_features(voxels)), 2),
  nrow = 8, ncol = n_features(voxels)
)

frame <- fmri_frame(
  assays = list(bold = bold),
  observations = data.frame(
    .obs_id = sprintf("vol-%02d", 1:8),
    run_id = rep(c("run-1", "run-2"), each = 4),
    TR = 2,
    motion = round(runif(8), 2)
  ),
  space = voxels
)
frame
```

The volume space gives each voxel inside the mask (its *support*; here every
voxel) a feature ID and a row of metadata: its linear index and grid
coordinates. `features()` returns that table for a frame.

```{r tables}
head(features(frame), 3)
```

The matrix itself is never trusted for identity. Had `bold` carried row names
that disagreed with `.obs_id`, construction would have failed rather than pick
one.

## Select by ID or by metadata

Square brackets take IDs on either axis and return a *view*: a lightweight
object that records which rows and columns of the frame it stands for, in the
order you asked. Reading a view returns a matrix labelled with those IDs.

```{r select-id}
view <- frame[c("vol-08", "vol-01"), c("voxel-5", "voxel-2")]
collect_assay(view)
```

When you know a property rather than an ID, `filter_observations()` evaluates
an expression against the observation table and `select_features()` against
the feature table.

```{r select-metadata}
run_2 <- filter_observations(frame, run_id == "run-2")
observation_ids(run_2)

still <- filter_observations(frame, motion < 0.5)
observation_ids(still)

top_slice <- select_features(frame, k == 2)
feature_ids(top_slice)
```

Views compose, and the feature space follows the selection: a view's space is
the original volume restricted to the selected voxels, in the selected order.

```{r select-compose}
corner <- top_slice[, c("voxel-18", "voxel-10")]
space(corner)
```

Selectors that are ambiguous or invalid are refused with a structured error:
a repeated ID, an unknown ID, or positive and negative positions mixed.

```{r select-errors, error = TRUE}
frame[c("vol-01", "vol-01"), ]
frame[, "voxel-99"]
frame[c(1, -2), ]
```

## Views are lazy

A view stores a selection, not values. To see that nothing is read until you
ask, wrap the matrix in `counting_source()`, which counts every read that
reaches it, and build a frame over it.

```{r lazy}
counted <- counting_source(bold)
lazy <- fmri_frame(
  assays = list(bold = counted),
  observations = observations(frame),
  space = voxels
)

lazy_run_1 <- filter_observations(lazy, run_id == "run-1")
run_1_pair <- lazy_run_1[, c("voxel-1", "voxel-2")]
source_counts(counted)$reads

values <- collect_assay(run_1_pair)
source_counts(counted)[c("reads", "values")]
```

Filtering and subsetting read nothing. `collect_assay()` read once, and only
the eight values the view stands for. With a file-backed frame, that is the
difference between reading a few voxels and reading every volume.

`collect_assay()` also estimates the memory a read needs and checks it against
a budget before reading, so a request that would not fit fails early.

```{r budget, error = TRUE}
collect_assay(frame, memory_budget = 10)
```

## Inspect without reading

`explain()` summarises a frame or view without reading any values: its shape,
whether its IDs are durable, its space, and, for each assay, the source behind
it and what reading it would cost.

```{r explain}
explain(run_2)
```

The two digests identify the frame's structure and its meaning;
`vignette("persistence-and-import")` explains them.

## Runs and timing

A frame stores no acquisition timing of its own. When its observations are
volumes acquired in runs, that is recorded in the observation table: a run
column, an optional `TR` in seconds (constant within a run), and an optional
logical `censor` column. `temporal_schema()` reads those columns and checks
them.

```{r temporal}
schema <- temporal_schema(frame)
schema
```

The run column is found automatically (`scan_id`, then `run_id`); pass
`run_col =` to choose another. With the `fmrihrf` package installed,
`as_sampling_frame()` converts the schema into the `sampling_frame` that HRF
and design-matrix code expects.

```{r sampling-frame-note, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !has_fmrihrf}
note("fmrihrf")
```

```{r sampling-frame, eval = has_fmrihrf}
as_sampling_frame(frame)
```

The schema is derived from the rows each time, so a filtered view describes
itself correctly.

```{r temporal-view}
temporal_schema(still)$run_lengths
```

A view whose runs are interleaved is a legal frame, but a sampling frame
cannot represent it, so the conversion refuses rather than reorder the rows
behind your back.

```{r temporal-interleaved, error = TRUE}
interleaved <- frame[c("vol-01", "vol-05", "vol-02"), ]
as_sampling_frame(interleaved)
```

Frames without runs, such as a matrix of beta estimates, are just as valid;
for them `has_temporal_schema()` is `FALSE`.

## IDs that last

IDs you supply, like `vol-01`, and IDs the constructors and importers make
are *durable*: the same data always gets the same IDs, so a frame can be saved
and compared with another. For throwaway work you can ask for *ephemeral*
IDs, which are random and visibly marked. A frame that has them cannot be
saved until they are replaced.

```{r ephemeral, error = TRUE}
scratch <- fmri_frame(
  assays = list(bold = bold),
  observations = axis_frame(data.frame(x = 1:8), id_policy = "ephemeral"),
  space = voxels
)
observation_ids(scratch)[1]
ids_are_durable(scratch)
write_frame(scratch, tempfile(fileext = ".h5"))
```

## Bind frames along observations

`bind_observations()` stacks frames that share a feature space. The result is
lazy: each row is still read from its original source. Rows follow the order
of the operands, IDs must not collide, and the spaces must be the same space,
not merely the same size.

```{r bind}
run_1 <- filter_observations(frame, run_id == "run-1")
both <- bind_observations(run_2, run_1)
observation_ids(both)
temporal_schema(both)$run_lengths
```

Frame-level metadata must match by default. With `metadata_policy = "merge"`,
records are combined, and only a genuine conflict is an error.

```{r bind-metadata, error = TRUE}
site_a <- fmri_frame(
  assays = list(bold = bold[1:4, ]),
  observations = observations(frame)[1:4, ],
  space = voxels,
  metadata = list(site = "A", scanner = list(vendor = "X"))
)
site_b <- fmri_frame(
  assays = list(bold = bold[5:8, ]),
  observations = observations(frame)[5:8, ],
  space = voxels,
  metadata = list(site = "A", scanner = list(field = "3T"))
)

bind_observations(site_a, site_b)

merged <- bind_observations(site_a, site_b, metadata_policy = "merge")
frame_metadata(merged)
```

Every bind is recorded in the frame's provenance.

```{r bind-provenance}
provenance(merged)
```

A frame over a different volume is refused even when the dimensions match.

```{r bind-space, error = TRUE}
other <- fmri_frame(
  assays = list(bold = bold[1:4, ]),
  observations = observations(frame)[1:4, ],
  space = volume_space(dim = c(3, 3, 2), template = "other")
)
bind_observations(site_a, other)
```

## What a frame promises

These are the package's contracts, from its
[data model](https://github.com/bbuchsbaum/fmridataset/blob/main/inst/architecture/ADR-001-canonical-data-model.md),
stated as behaviour you can rely on.

- **Two axes, always.** An assay is observations by features. Conditions,
  runs, and covariates are columns of the observation table, never a third
  dimension.
- **Every assay shares the axes.** All assays in a frame have the same
  observation and feature IDs, in the same order.
- **IDs are stable and explicit.** Subsetting, reordering, and binding carry
  IDs through unchanged. Nothing regenerates them, and nothing aligns by
  position.
- **Spatial identity is semantic.** Two spaces are the same only when their
  type, digest, and ordered feature IDs agree. Matching dimensions are not
  evidence.
- **Ambiguity fails early.** Repeated selectors, conflicting labels,
  disagreeing metadata, and colliding IDs raise structured errors instead of
  being resolved by a rule you did not choose.
- **Reading is lazy and bounded.** Views and binds read no assay values.
  Reading goes through an explicit memory budget, and `explain()` reports the
  cost first.
- **Descriptions, not handles.** A frame holds descriptions of its sources,
  never open files or connections, so it can be saved and rebuilt elsewhere.
